intro: Two kinds of football grew up in the 1800s. One grew on American college lawns and became the game played on a gridiron. The other was written down in a London tavern in 1863 and became soccer, played on a pitch. Both started with older town games that had crowds, a ball and no written rules.

In this unit you will meet the students, lawyers, teachers and presidents who wrote the rules down. You will see how meetings in Springfield, London, Chicago and Paris turned local games into shared codes. You will also see who was shut out, such as women's teams banned in England in 1921, and when doors opened.

By the end, you can name the bodies that keep each game's rules, like the NCAA, IFAB, FIFA and the IHSA. You can put key dates in order. You can explain why a school field and a World Cup stadium follow the same written rules.
bigQuestion: How did two games with old roots get written rule books, governing bodies and fields that schools and nations could share?

title: School Fields and World Pitches

chapters.title: The Gridiron Beside the School
chapters.bigQuestion: How did rough games on college lawns turn into a written game with a governing body and a field every town could build?

story.title: Painted Grass on a Friday
story.kicker: Before anyone sits down, the bleachers face a rectangle of painted grass.
paragraphs: It is Friday afternoon in a small Illinois town. Maya helps her grandfather carry a cooler to the high school field. The bleachers are empty. They all face a long rectangle of grass with white lines painted across it every five yards.

"Why so many lines?" Maya asks. Her grandfather says the lines are old. College rule makers added lines like them in the 1880s. From the stands, the field looked like a cooking grill. People began calling it a gridiron.

A metal sign by the gate says the field belongs to the school district. Taxes and bond votes paid for the grass, the lights and the seats. On game nights the band, the families and the whole town come here.

Maya's grandfather remembers his own school days. Back then, Illinois had no state football playoffs. The Illinois High School Association, called the IHSA, started them in 1974. Now teams from the whole state chase one title each fall.
story.think: Who do you think paid for the field, the lights and the bleachers, and why would a town want one?

lessons.title: Town Games in Old England
lessons.mainIdea: Long before rule books, English towns played huge, rough ball games in the streets, and leaders sometimes banned them.
reading: In medieval England, whole villages played *folk football*. Hundreds of people chased one ball through streets and fields. The goals could be a mile apart. There was no written rule book, and each town had its own customs.

The games were so wild that leaders tried to stop them. In 1314, the Lord Mayor of London banned football in the city in the name of King Edward II. Later kings passed more bans. The games kept going anyway.

Many towns played on *Shrove Tuesday*, a holiday before the Christian season of Lent. The town of Ashbourne in Derbyshire still holds a two-day Shrovetide game. Its two goals stand about three miles apart.

a holiday before Lent, when many English towns held a big ball game

lessons.title: Rutgers and Princeton, 1869
lessons.mainIdea: The first game between two American colleges was played in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on November 6, 1869.
reading: On November 6, 1869, students from *Rutgers* and Princeton met on a field in New Brunswick, New Jersey. It was the first football game between two American colleges. Each side had 25 players.
The game looked more like soccer than today's American football. Players kicked and batted a round ball. They could not pick it up and run. Rutgers won, six goals to four.
About a hundred people watched. The Rutgers student newspaper, the *Targum*, wrote a report of the game. That report is one reason historians know the date and the score.

lessons.title: McGill Visits Harvard, 1874
lessons.mainIdea: In 1874 Harvard played McGill University of Montreal and liked McGill's rugby-style game, which let players carry the ball.
reading: In May 1874, a team from *McGill University* in Montreal, Canada, came to Cambridge, Massachusetts. They played two games against Harvard. McGill played a game like *rugby*, where players could pick up the ball and run.
The two schools split the rules. One game used Harvard's rules. The other used McGill's. Harvard players liked carrying the ball, so they kept the rugby style.
Harvard then played Yale in 1875 using rules close to rugby. Other eastern colleges soon followed. A game from Canada and England had changed the American college game.

lessons.title: A Meeting at the Massasoit House
lessons.mainIdea: In 1876 college students met in Springfield, Massachusetts, and started the Intercollegiate Football Association with rugby-based rules.
reading: In November 1876, students from four colleges met in Springfield, Massachusetts. They came from Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Columbia. The meeting was held at the Massasoit House hotel. They wanted one set of rules for games between their schools.
The meeting started the *Intercollegiate Football Association*. It was a group of colleges that agreed on shared rules. The group used the rugby rules of England as its base.

Rugby rules then put 15 players on each side. Yale's students wanted fewer players. That argument went on for a few years. It shows that a *convention*, a meeting to agree on rules, did not settle every question at once.

lessons.title: Walter Camp's Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Walter Camp of Yale led rule changes in 1880 and 1882 that turned a rugby-style game into American football and gave the field its gridiron lines.
reading: *Walter Camp* played for Yale and later guided its team. He sat on college rule committees for many years. In 1880 his group cut each side to 11 players. It also replaced rugby's scrum with a *line of scrimmage*, where each play starts.
In 1882 a new rule said a team had three tries, called downs, to gain five yards. Officials needed to measure the ground. So lines were drawn across the field every five yards.
From above, the lines looked like a cooking grill, or gridiron. The name stuck. Camp is often called the father of American football. He also wrote a book called American Football in 1891.

lessons.title: William Henry Lewis, All-America
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 William Henry Lewis became the first Black player named to college football's All-America team.
reading: *William Henry Lewis* was born in Virginia in 1868. His parents had been enslaved. He studied at Amherst College and then at Harvard Law School. He played football at both schools.

Starting in 1889, sports writers picked an *All-America team*, a list of the best college players. Walter Camp helped choose it. In 1892 Lewis was named to the list. He was the first Black player chosen.

Few Black students could attend these colleges then. Lewis later became a lawyer. In 1911 he was named an Assistant Attorney General of the United States. He was one of the first Black Americans to hold such a high federal post.

lessons.title: The Hard Season of 1905
lessons.mainIdea: Many players were badly hurt or killed in 1905, and President Theodore Roosevelt pushed colleges to make football safer.
reading: By 1905, college football was a dangerous game. Players crashed together in big piles. Few wore helmets. Newspapers counted about 18 player deaths that season. Many more players were badly hurt.

Some leaders wanted to end football. Columbia University dropped the game in 1905. In October 1905, President *Theodore Roosevelt* invited men from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House. He asked them to make the game safer.

In November 1905, Harold Moore of Union College died in a game against New York University. Henry MacCracken led NYU. He called college leaders together to talk about *reform*. Reform means changing rules to fix a problem.

lessons.title: A Rule Body Called the NCAA
lessons.mainIdea: The 1905 crisis led to a new college rule body in 1906, renamed the NCAA in 1910, and to the forward pass becoming legal.
reading: Henry MacCracken's meetings led to a new group. In March 1906 it was formally set up as the *Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States*. About sixty colleges joined at the start.

In 1906 the rule makers changed football. They made the *forward pass* legal. They also made a team gain ten yards, not five, to keep the ball. Leaders hoped these changes would break up the dangerous piles.

In 1910 the group took a new name: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or *NCAA*. Today the NCAA runs rules and championships for many college sports. It began because of a safety crisis in one game.

lessons.title: A Conference Born in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 leaders of seven Midwest universities met in Chicago and started the conference now called the Big Ten.
reading: In January 1895, the presidents of seven universities met at the Palmer House hotel in Chicago. They came from Chicago, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, Northwestern, Purdue and Wisconsin. They wanted shared rules for college sports.
Their group became the Western Conference. A *conference* is a group of schools that play each other under shared rules. Today it is known as the Big Ten.

*Amos Alonzo Stagg* coached football at the University of Chicago from 1892 to 1932. The school's field was named Stagg Field. Chicago left the conference in 1946, but it was one of the group's first members.

The stadium is called *Memorial Stadium*. Its columns carry the names of Illinois students and graduates who died in the war. A *memorial* is a place or object built to remember people.

The stadium was dedicated on October 18, 1924. That day Red Grange of Illinois scored four touchdowns against Michigan in the first twelve minutes. The game made the new stadium famous across the country.

chapters.title: A Rectangle the World Can Share
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one short rule book, written in London in 1863, become a game that people in almost every country can play together?

story.title: Two Towns, One Rectangle
story.kicker: Two towns that do not share a language still share a rectangle.
paragraphs: On one side of a border, a team speaks Spanish. On the other side, a team speaks Portuguese. On Saturday they meet on a grass field. The coaches cannot understand each other's words. The players still know exactly where to stand for the start.

Both teams know the white lines. There is a halfway line, a center circle and a goal at each end. The lines come from Law 1 of the Laws of the Game. That law describes the field of play, and it is the same in every country.

The rule book began in London in 1863. It was short enough to print on a few pages. Sailors, students and workers carried copies across oceans. By 1904, soccer groups from seven European countries had formed FIFA in Paris.

Long before that rule book, people in China, Japan and England kicked balls in their own ways. The written laws did not invent kicking. They gave strangers one shared set of rules. That is why two towns without a shared language can play one game.
story.think: What does a written rule book let strangers do that they could not do without it?

lessons.title: Cuju and Kemari
lessons.mainIdea: People in China and Japan played kicking games with a ball many centuries before soccer's rules were written in England.
reading: In ancient China, people played *cuju*. The name means "kick ball." Records show it was played during the Han dynasty, more than 2,000 years ago. Soldiers played it for training, and later it was played at the royal court.
FIFA, the world soccer body, has called cuju the earliest form of football with written evidence. Cuju had its own goals and its own customs. It was not the same game as modern soccer.

In Japan, nobles played *kemari* more than 1,000 years ago. Players stood in a circle and kept a deerskin ball in the air. Kemari is still shown at some Kyoto shrines today. There is no winner in kemari.

an old Japanese court game where players keep a deerskin ball in the air

lessons.title: School Rules in England
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, English schools and clubs each wrote their own football rules, which made games between them hard.
reading: In the early 1800s, English boarding schools such as Eton, Harrow and Rugby each played football their own way. Some let players carry the ball. Others did not. Students who went on to university could not agree on one game.

In 1848, students at Cambridge University wrote the *Cambridge Rules*. They wanted players from different schools to share one set of rules. No full copy of the 1848 rules survives, but later versions do.
In 1857, Sheffield Football Club was started in the north of England. It is often called the oldest football *club* still playing. A year later, it wrote the Sheffield Rules for its own games.

lessons.title: A London Tavern, 1863
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association was founded at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on October 26, 1863, and it wrote the first laws of association football.
reading: On October 26, 1863, men from about a dozen London clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern. A lawyer named *Ebenezer Cobb Morley* had called the meeting. They founded the *Football Association*, called the FA.
Over several meetings they argued about carrying the ball and kicking other players' shins. In December 1863 they agreed on 13 laws. Those laws said players could not carry the ball in their hands.

The Blackheath club wanted carrying and shin kicking kept, so it left. Clubs that liked carrying later formed the Rugby Football Union in 1871. The FA's game was called *association football*. The word soccer comes from "association."

lessons.title: A Board to Guard the Laws
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886 the International Football Association Board, called IFAB, has decided the Laws of the Game.
reading: By the 1880s, England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland each had its own football association. Their rules did not always match. That caused arguments when their teams played each other.
On June 2, 1886, the four associations met in London. They formed the *International Football Association Board*, or *IFAB*. Its job is to keep one set of *Laws of the Game* for everyone.
FIFA joined IFAB in 1913. Today IFAB has eight votes. FIFA holds four, and the four British associations hold one each. A law can change only when at least six of the eight votes agree.

lessons.title: Balls in a Suitcase
lessons.mainIdea: Teachers, students and workers carried the rules of association football to South America in the late 1800s.
reading: British workers, sailors and teachers lived in many port cities in the 1800s. They brought balls and rule books with them. Local people watched, joined in and started their own clubs.

*Alexander Watson Hutton* was a Scottish teacher who moved to Buenos Aires, Argentina. In 1893 he helped found the Argentine Association Football League. He is often called the father of Argentine football.

*Charles Miller* was born in São Paulo, Brazil, in 1874. He went to school in England and learned the game there. In 1894 he came home with footballs and a copy of the rules. He helped start organized soccer in São Paulo.

reading: On May 21, 1904, football leaders met in Paris, France. They founded *FIFA*, the Fédération Internationale de Football Association. In English, that means International Federation of Association Football.

The seven founding members came from France, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland. England's FA joined in 1905. A *federation* is a group of separate bodies that agree to work together.
FIFA agreed to play by the Laws of the Game kept by IFAB. Today FIFA has more than 200 member associations. That is more members than the United Nations has countries.

lessons.title: Uruguay Hosts the World, 1930
lessons.mainIdea: The first FIFA World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won the final against Argentina.
reading: FIFA president *Jules Rimet* of France wanted a tournament for national teams. In 1930 the first *World Cup* was held in Uruguay, in South America. That year was the 100th anniversary of Uruguay's first constitution.

Uruguay built the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo for the event. The name means Centenary Stadium. Thirteen teams took part. Only four came from Europe, because the trip by ship took about two weeks.
On July 30, 1930, Uruguay beat Argentina 4 to 2 in the final. The United States team also played and reached the semifinals. Today the World Cup is held every four years.

lessons.title: Women Shut Out, Then Back
lessons.mainIdea: England's FA banned women's games from its members' grounds in 1921 and did not lift the ban until 1971.
reading: During World War I, many women worked in factories in England. Some formed football teams. The *Dick, Kerr Ladies* came from a factory in Preston. On Boxing Day 1920, about 53,000 people watched them play at Goodison Park in Liverpool.

On December 5, 1921, the FA made a new rule. It said football was "quite unsuitable for females." Member clubs could no longer let women's teams use their grounds. This was a *ban*, a rule that stops people from doing something.
Women kept playing on smaller fields. The FA lifted the ban in 1971. FIFA held the first Women's World Cup in China in 1991. The United States won it.

lessons.title: Law 1: The Field of Play
lessons.mainIdea: Law 1 of the Laws of the Game lets a soccer field be many sizes, as long as it is a rectangle with the right markings.
reading: A soccer field is called a *pitch*. Law 1 of the Laws of the Game describes it. It must be a rectangle. The long sides are touchlines. Each one is a *touchline*. The short sides are goal lines.
Law 1 gives a range of sizes, not one size. A pitch may be 90 to 120 meters long. That lets a village, a school or a big city stadium all follow the same law.

Some parts never change. Every goal is 8 yards wide and 8 feet high, or 7.32 meters by 2.44 meters. Those sizes come from the British measures of the 1800s. They were kept when the laws spread around the world.

The *United States Soccer Federation*, called U.S. Soccer, runs the sport's national teams. It has had its headquarters in Chicago since 1991. Its offices are in an old mansion on Prairie Avenue.

Chicago also has a professional club, the Chicago Fire. The team is named for the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. It played its first season in 1998 and won Major League Soccer's championship that same year.

lessons.title: State Titles for Boys and Girls
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first boys soccer state champion in 1972 and its first girls soccer state champion in 1988.
reading: Illinois high schools played soccer for years without a state title. The IHSA held its first boys soccer *state series* in the fall of 1972. A state series is a set of playoff rounds that ends with one champion.
Also in 1972, Congress passed *Title IX*. This federal law says schools that get federal money cannot shut students out of programs because of sex. Schools began adding more sports for girls.
Girls soccer grew in Illinois through the 1970s and 1980s. The IHSA crowned its first girls soccer state champion in 1988. Today boys play in the fall and girls play in the spring.
